title: Pluggable interceptors and policies
idea: An extensible `ApiClient` is assembled by a builder from a base transport, a chain of interceptors and a retry strategy, so new behaviour arrives as a new class.
points: An `Interceptor` wraps each attempt: logging, request ids, auth, or a breaker.
The builder wraps the transport inside-out, so the first interceptor added runs first.
A policy decorator such as `RetryAfterPolicy` adds rules around an existing strategy.
`build()` rejects incomplete configuration before any request is sent.

Pattern
Added without edits
rows: Honour 429 and the server's wait hint
hero.caption: Each row is a seam. A new provider or rule is a new class plugged into a seam; the retry loop never changes.

code.title: Builder, chain, decorator
code.caption: A payments client gets request ids, logging and Retry-After support, all added as classes. A client with no policy is refused. Backoff still checks safeToRepeat.

walk.text: The fake server answers 429 with a 2000 ms hint, then 200.
Configuration reads as a sentence: transport, two interceptors, and a wrapped policy with a 5000 ms hint cap.
A trimmed loop: prints the wait instead of sleeping, and has no deadline. It knows nothing about 429.
Refuse a client with no retry policy at build time.
Wrap from the last interceptor to the first, so the first added runs outermost.
The decorator treats 429 as retryable and prefers the server's wait, capped, over its own.
Each attempt gets a fresh request id on a copied request.

pitfalls: Do not add `if (service == ...)` branches to the loop; configure a different client.
Cap any server Retry-After hint; a huge value can stall your own caller.
Mind interceptor order: a breaker outside logging hides refused calls from the log.

quiz.q: What does the first line of Extensible print?
quiz.why: RequestId was added first, so it runs outside Logging. Logging sees the stamped request, and prints after the 429 arrives.

takeaway: Extend the client with new classes, never new branches in the loop.
